input.notes:
Big reversal on #1 tonight's results refine, not confirm, last week's alarm: order_status_history shows 100% coverage of cancellations across every one of the 50 tenants printed — Tidewick DOES have a timestamped record of every cancellation, just not in generic audit_log. But matching_rows_with_actor is 0 for every tenant — the WHO is missing even though the WHEN is solid. That's a much narrower, more precise finding than "we can't reconstruct order history." Invoice voids turn out to not exist at all (0 ever), so that's a non-issue; but 85 "uncollectible" write-offs across 11 tenants have genuinely 0% audit trail and no purpose-built history table standing in — that's the real, confirmed financial-document gap. And the churn-session risk mostly evaporates: all never-revoked sessions on all 9 churned tenants are already naturally expired (0 still valid) — so the real residual churn risk is just account status (100% of users, all 9 tenants) plus the 2 tenants with a live API key/webhook found last week.

With #1 and #3 now reasonably well-characterized, tonight I'm clearing Henrik's remaining two questions: whether the "no actor" gap in order_status_history is specific to cancellations or systemic across all transitions (quick, sharpens the #1 story), what actually stands in for shopper MFA (oauth-linked login vs raw password), and who specifically holds the oldest active API keys so we can judge concentration/sensitivity for #4.

columns: method category ('OAuth-linked' = has ≥1 oauth_accounts row, 'password-only' = no oauth_accounts row)

requests.grain: one row per api_keys row in the '4+ years' active age bucket (created_at more than 4 years before 2026-01-05, status = 'active')
columns: associated rate_limits scope, if any (limit_scope from rate_limits where api_key_id matches)
associated rate_limits max_requests per window, if any
requests.details: Source: api_keys where status = 'active' and created_at < (2026-01-05 minus 4 years), left-joined to tenants and to rate_limits (api_key_id = api_keys.id) for scope context — if a key has multiple rate_limits rows, include all of them as additional rows for that key (or note in the report if a key has more than one scope). Order by age in days descending (oldest first), tenant name as tie-break. Cap at 50 rows; note total matching keys (expect ~76 based on last week's age-bucket report).
builds_on: Active API key age distribution (rotation hygiene)

input.notes:
Night 3 sharpened every thread nicely. Report 1 confirms the "no actor" gap in order_status_history is NOT cancellation-specific — it's 0.0% across every single status transition (pending, paid, fulfilled, cancelled, refunded; 150k+ rows, ~118 tenants) — a systemic table-wide property, not a narrow bug. Report 2 gives the clean #2 number: 88.3% of shoppers (9,910) are password-only with literally no backup factor, vs. 11.7% who at least inherit some protection from an OAuth provider — and recent-activity rates are nearly identical between the two groups (47.9% vs 46.9%), so OAuth adoption isn't just an artifact of inactive accounts. Report 3 is the most consequential: the long-lived (4+ year) active keys are dominated by integration-type keys ("ERP sync", "Accounting sync", "Warehouse management sync", "Marketplace product feed sync") nearly all carrying `limit_scope = admin_api`, used daily (every row shows ~5 days since last use, clustered right at month-end — looks like a nightly batch job), and they belong to our largest, most revenue-concentrated merchants (Cragsley Outfitters, Marrowby & Vane both appear with 4-5 such keys each). That's "old + broad + important account" together, exactly what Henrik flagged as the real risk combination.

Last night of the cycle — I want three closing numbers rather than opening new threads: (1) the full scope tally across all 76 old keys (the printed list only showed 50), (2) whether admin_api scope is concentrated in old keys specifically or is just how all integration keys are scoped regardless of age (tells us if "old+broad" is a rotation failure or a design norm), and (3) closing the loop between the churn and API-key findings by checking whether the 2 active keys sitting on churned tenants carry that same elevated scope.

requests.title: Scope tally across all 76 long-lived (4+ year) active API keys
requests.question: Of all 76 active API keys that are 4+ years old, how many actually carry the broad 'admin_api' rate-limit scope versus no scope recorded at all — the full count, not just the 50 printed last night?
requests.grain: one row per distinct limit_scope value (including a 'no scope recorded' category for keys with no matching rate_limits row)
columns: scope category ('admin_api', any other distinct limit_scope values found, or 'no scope recorded')
distinct key count (count distinct api_keys.id, not rate_limits rows)
requests.details: Source: api_keys where status = 'active' and created_at < (2026-01-05 minus 4 years) — the same 76-key population as last night's detail report — left-joined to rate_limits on api_key_id. Group by rate_limits.limit_scope (treat null, i.e. no matching rate_limits row, as its own category 'no scope recorded'). Count DISTINCT api_keys.id per group so a key is not double-counted if it somehow has more than one rate_limits row. Order by distinct key count descending, scope category as tie-break.
builds_on: Detail list of the oldest active API keys (4+ years), by tenant

requests.title: Is admin_api scope concentrated in old keys, or standard across all ages?
requests.question: Are broadly-scoped (admin_api) keys specifically a feature of our oldest, longest-unrotated keys, or is that scope just how every integration key is set up regardless of age — i.e. is 'old + broad' a rotation failure or simply the norm?
requests.grain: one row per active-key age bucket (the same 5 buckets used previously: under 90 days, 90 days-1 year, 1-2 years, 2-4 years, 4+ years)
columns: of those, keys with no matching rate_limits row ('no scope recorded')
requests.details: Source: api_keys where status = 'active', bucketed by age (2026-01-05 minus created_at) into the same 5 fixed ranges as the earlier age-distribution report, left-joined to rate_limits on api_key_id (count distinct api_keys.id per bucket to avoid double-counting if a key has multiple rate_limits rows). Order rows by bucket from youngest to oldest in the fixed sequence (not alphabetical), so the trend is readable top to bottom.
builds_on: Active API key age distribution (rotation hygiene)

content.text:
**To:** Henrik Aalto, CISO
**From:** Noah Fischer, Analytics
**Re:** Deletion-audit scope, churn deprovisioning, shopper MFA, old keys — answers

Henrik — here's what this week's follow-ups found, in the order you asked.

**#1 Deletion-audit gap: narrower than feared, but two real holes.**
A full census of every soft-deletable table (30 tables) shows only two have ever actually had a deletion: products (615 rows, 91 merchants, still 0% logged in audit_log) and users (39 rows, 69.2% logged). The other 28 show zero deletions ever — that's not evidence they're fine, just untested.
Orders are better news than last week suggested: the purpose-built `order_status_history` table shows **100% coverage** of every cancellation, and every status change, across 90–118 merchants — we can reliably show *when* an order changed state. But *who* cannot be shown: across 150k+ transitions, every status, every merchant, the actor field is populated **0.0% of the time**, with no exceptions. That's a systemic property of the table, not a cancellation-specific bug.
A smaller, confirmed gap: invoices are never formally "voided" (0 ever), but 85 "uncollectible" write-offs across 11 merchants have zero audit trail and no equivalent history table standing in. **Confident** in all four numbers.

**#3 Churn deprovisioning: real, but the live exposure is narrow.**
Every user on all 9 churned tenants is still `status = active` — universal, not limited to Owner/Admin as first reported. But exploitable risk is small: all "never-revoked" sessions on every churned tenant have already naturally expired (0 still valid). Two tenants (Dewdrop Studio, Aurum & Ash) still run one live API key each, both carrying `admin_api` scope and used in the last 5 days via what looks like an automated nightly ERP sync — a genuinely live, broadly-scoped credential still talking to a merchant who no longer pays us. **Confident**: the fix is a churn trigger that disables accounts and revokes keys/webhooks; those two tenants need attention now.

**#2 Shopper MFA: a real gap, not overstated.**
88.3% of shoppers (9,910) are password-only with no backup of any kind; only 11.7% get indirect protection via an OAuth login, and even that group has 0% confirmed MFA. Recent-activity rates are nearly identical across both groups (47.9% vs 46.9%), so this isn't just inactive accounts inflating one side. **Confident** this is a genuine liability.

**#4 Old API keys: broad access is the norm, not an age-driven drift.**
53 of 76 long-lived (4+ year) active keys (69.7%, 25 merchants) carry `admin_api` scope. Scope breaks down similarly across every age bucket (70–100%), so broad access isn't creeping in with age — it's simply how integration keys are provisioned platform-wide. The real risk is that these broad keys never rotate, and they concentrate on our biggest accounts: Cragsley Outfitters and Marrowby & Vane each run 4–5 of them.

**Caveats:** The 28 "zero deletions ever" tables prove absence of data, not absence of risk — don't read them as clean. Every key's "5 days since last use" timestamp clusters within minutes of each other on Dec 31, which smells like one nightly batch job rather than genuinely independent usage — worth confirming with engineering before treating usage as fully reassuring.

**Next steps:** (1) apply the churn-trigger fix immediately to the 2 live-key tenants, then design it platform-wide; (2) decide whether `order_status_history` needs an actor column — a one-table fix with outsized audit value; (3) scope a rotation mandate specifically for `admin_api`-scoped keys, starting with Cragsley and Marrowby.
